scenes.animation: Zippy cuts a parallelogram-shaped paper along one diagonal with cartoon scissors. The two triangle halves fly up, spin, and land exactly on top of each other with a 'click'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I cut my parallelogram in half and the pieces are identical. Did I cheat?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, you discovered a theorem. A diagonal always splits a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.

scenes.animation: Parallelogram ABCD with arrow marks showing AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC. The definition appears: 'Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides parallel'. Diagonal AC is drawn in green.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let's prove that diagonal AC divides it into two congruent triangles.

scenes.animation: Proof built step by step. With AC as transversal, alternate angles light up in pairs: '∠BCA = ∠DAC (AD ∥ BC)', '∠BAC = ∠DCA (AB ∥ DC)', 'AC = CA (common)', '∴ △ABC ≅ △CDA (ASA)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: AC is a transversal to the parallel lines AD and BC. So angle BCA equals angle DAC, as alternate angles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: AC is also a transversal to AB and DC. So angle BAC equals angle DCA.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: AC is common. So triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA by ASA.

scenes.animation: From the congruent triangles, CPCT arrows pop out: 'AB = DC', 'AD = BC', '∠B = ∠D'. A second card shows '∠A = ∠C'. Then a flip card: 'Converse: opposite sides equal ⇒ parallelogram; opposite angles equal ⇒ parallelogram'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By CPCT, AB equals DC and AD equals BC. So in a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Similarly, angle B equals angle D, and using the other diagonal, angle A equals angle C. Opposite angles are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converses are true too. If each pair of opposite sides is equal, or each pair of opposite angles is equal, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a chalkboard, line by line: 'ABCD is a parallelogram, ∠A = 70°', '∠C = ∠A = 70° (opposite angles)', '∠A + ∠B = 180° (co-interior, AD ∥ BC)', '∠B = 180° − 70° = 110°', '∠D = ∠B = 110°', 'Check: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360° ✓'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If angle A is 70 degrees, are all the angles 70?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Only the opposite one. Angle C equals angle A, so angle C is 70 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angles A and B are co-interior angles between parallel lines, so they add up to 180. Angle B is 180 minus 70, which is 110 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angle D equals angle B, which is 110 degrees. Check: 70 plus 110 plus 70 plus 110 is 360. Correct.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary. Name the reason as co-interior angles.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the two matching paper triangles: '1. A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles', '2. Opposite sides equal; opposite angles equal (and converses)', '3. Adjacent angles add to 180°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal, and the converses hold.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180 degrees.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So I didn't cheat. I proved!

scenes.animation: A kite-flying scene on a rooftop at Makar Sankranti. Zippy's rhombus-shaped kite has two sticks crossing inside; a magnifier shows the sticks crossing at exactly 90° and cutting each other in half.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why does the kite-maker tie the sticks exactly at their middles, at a right angle?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because that is what the diagonals of a rhombus do. Let's see why.

scenes.animation: Parallelogram ABCD with diagonals AC and BD crossing at O. Half-segments get tick marks: OA = OC with one tick, OB = OD with two ticks. Theorem box: 'The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangles AOB and COD, AB equals CD, and the alternate angles at A and C, and at B and D, are equal. So they are congruent by ASA, which gives OA equals OC and OB equals OD.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse is also true: if the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a parallelogram.

scenes.animation: Rhombus ABCD with all sides ticked equal and diagonals meeting at O. Proof lines appear: 'OA = OC (diagonals bisect)', 'AB = CB (sides of rhombus)', 'OB = OB (common)', '∴ △AOB ≅ △COB (SSS)', '∠AOB = ∠COB (CPCT)', '∠AOB + ∠COB = 180° (linear pair)', '∴ ∠AOB = 90°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal. Let's show its diagonals are perpendicular.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: OA equals OC, since the diagonals bisect each other. AB equals CB, as sides of the rhombus. OB is common.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COB by SSS, and angle AOB equals angle COB by CPCT.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: These two angles form a linear pair, so each is 180 divided by 2, which is 90 degrees.

scenes.animation: Worked example: rhombus with diagonals labelled AC = 10 cm, BD = 24 cm. Lines build: 'OA = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm', 'OB = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm', '∠AOB = 90°', 'AB² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169', 'AB = 13 cm'. A kite string measures 13 cm with a tick.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My kite sticks are 10 and 24 centimetres long. How long is each side?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Half of 10 is 5, and half of 24 is 12. They meet at a right angle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By Pythagoras, side squared is 5 squared plus 12 squared, which is 25 plus 144, or 169. So each side is 13 centimetres.

scenes.animation: A rectangle appears with equal diagonals glowing, next to the rhombus. A comparison card: 'Rectangle: each angle 90°, diagonals equal', 'Rhombus: diagonals perpendicular', 'Square: both'. An 'EXAM TIP' sticker flashes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A rectangle is a parallelogram with one angle 90 degrees. Then every angle becomes 90 degrees, and its diagonals are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: when proving a special parallelogram, first show it is a parallelogram, then prove the extra property.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the kite fluttering: '1. Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other (and converse)', '2. Rhombus: diagonals are perpendicular bisectors', '3. Rectangle: all angles 90°, diagonals equal'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and the converse is true.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a rectangle has all angles 90 degrees and equal diagonals.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Kite approved by geometry. Launching!

scenes.animation: A triangular slice of pizza sits on a plate. Zippy marks the midpoints of two edges with ketchup dots and joins them with a ketchup line; a ruler pops up showing the line is parallel to the crust and exactly half its length.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I joined two midpoints and got a line parallel to the third side. And it's exactly half as long!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the mid-point theorem. It works for every triangle.

scenes.animation: Triangle ABC with E the midpoint of AB and F the midpoint of AC, both ticked. Segment EF glows. Theorem box: 'EF ∥ BC and EF = ½ BC'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mid-point theorem: the line segment joining the mid-points of any two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Also, it is half of the third side.

scenes.animation: Proof builds step by step: a line through C parallel to BA is drawn, and EF is extended to meet it at D. Lines appear: 'AF = CF (F is mid-point)', '∠AFE = ∠CFD (vertically opposite)', '∠EAF = ∠DCF (alternate angles, BA ∥ CD)', '∴ △AEF ≅ △CDF (ASA)', 'EF = DF and AE = CD (CPCT)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Draw a line through C parallel to BA, and extend EF to meet it at D.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangles AEF and CDF: AF equals CF. Angle AFE equals angle CFD, vertically opposite. Angle EAF equals angle DCF, as alternate angles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the triangles are congruent by ASA. By CPCT, EF equals DF and AE equals CD.

scenes.animation: Quadrilateral BCDE is shaded. Lines appear: 'BE = AE = CD', 'BE ∥ CD', '∴ BCDE is a parallelogram', '∴ ED ∥ BC and ED = BC', 'EF = ½ ED = ½ BC'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now BE equals AE, which equals CD. And BE is parallel to CD.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel is a parallelogram. So BCDE is a parallelogram.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So ED is parallel to BC and equal to it. Since EF is half of ED, EF is half of BC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse: a line through the mid-point of one side, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.

scenes.animation: Worked example: triangle with sides 6 cm, 7 cm, 8 cm. Midpoints are joined to form a small inner triangle. Lines build: 'Inner sides: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm, 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 cm, 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm', 'Perimeter = 3 + 3.5 + 4 = 10.5 cm'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: a triangle has sides 6, 7 and 8 centimetres. Find the perimeter of the triangle formed by joining the mid-points of its sides.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each inner side is half the side it is parallel to. So they are 3, 3.5 and 4 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Perimeter is 3 plus 3.5 plus 4, which is 10.5 centimetres. That's half of the original perimeter, 21.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: always state both parts, parallel and half, when you quote the theorem.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the ketchup-line pizza: '1. Mid-points joined ⇒ parallel to third side', '2. That segment = ½ the third side', '3. Converse: line through a mid-point, parallel to a side, bisects the third side'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides is parallel to the third side.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: it is half the length of the third side.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a line through a mid-point, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And now I'll prove that pizza is half gone.
